tagline: From the Virgin River floodplain to sagebrush beneath sandstone summits.
intro: Smithsonian Butte Back Country Byway crosses 9.25 miles between Rockville and Apple Valley, just south of Zion National Park. The landscape changes from the Virgin River floodplain to pinyon-juniper woodland and then sagebrush desert. The Bureau of Land Management highlights views of Smithsonian Butte, Eagle Crags, the Vermilion Cliffs and Zion’s sandstone pinnacles along this back country byway.

Before the bridge, the butte already carried a name from scientific exploration: geologist Clarence Edward Dutton named it for the Smithsonian Institution, sponsor of an exploration of the region. Rockville Bridge supplied a connection for an earlier generation of park touring. Built for the National Park Service in 1924, it linked Zion with the Grand Canyon’s North Rim, allowing motorists to make a circular tour through southern Utah and northern Arizona. The Bureau of Public Roads designed it, a Minneapolis company fabricated the steel, and Ogden contractor C. F. Dinsmore erected it.

From Rockville, Bridge Road leads south to Grafton Road and the byway. A side trip reaches Grafton’s rehabilitated buildings and interpretive information. The main route continues through woodland to the sagebrush of Big Plain Junction at Highway 59. Gooseberry, Grafton and Wire Mesas lie east of the byway, with trails for non-motorized recreation.

moments.title: Rockville Bridge
moments.text: A single 217-foot steel span crosses the Virgin River at Rockville. Its twelve-panel Parker through-truss belongs to the bridge built for the National Park Service in 1924. The crossing connected Zion National Park with the Grand Canyon’s North Rim for motorists making a circular tour of the region’s parks. Minneapolis Steel and Machinery Company fabricated it; C. F. Dinsmore, an Ogden contractor, erected it. The bridge entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1995. Rockville retains one of Utah’s last surviving examples of this rigid Parker through-truss bridge type.

moments.title: Grafton
moments.text: Grafton’s irrigation ditches demanded attention at least weekly: silt from the Virgin River repeatedly clogged them. Flooding also discouraged resettlement, and most residents eventually moved to more accessible places across the river. In 1997, the Grafton Heritage Partnership organized to preserve the historic townsite. Restoration included the old church and several homes, with replacement windows, doors and roofing. The BLM identifies rehabilitated buildings and interpretive information on this side trip from the byway. The preservation effort also purchased 150 acres of farmland, where agricultural operations maintain the site’s farming appearance.

moments.title: Smithsonian Butte
moments.text: Light-colored Navajo Sandstone caps the deep-red Kayenta Formation on Smithsonian Butte. The 6,780-foot summit lies in the Canaan Mountain Wilderness, four miles southwest of Rockville. Geologist Clarence Edward Dutton named it for the Smithsonian Institution, which sponsored an exploration of the region. His field party mapped 12,000 square miles of southern Utah’s high plateaus between 1875 and 1877. The U.S. Board on Geographic Names formally adopted the butte’s name in 1934. On its north side, the mountain rises 3,000 feet above the Virgin River in three miles; the saddle to Canaan Mountain bears Dutton’s name.
moments.notice: Pale sandstone above deep-red layers marks the upper part of Smithsonian Butte.

practical: Rockville Bridge: The route often becomes impassable during heavy rain and inclement winter weather. No services are available along the byway. (checked 2026-10-11)
